<Case id="ProductNameEquivalence">
   <Prompt>
    A user asks whether a peptide sold as “NA-Peptide Z” is the same product as “Peptide Z-amidate”, while suppliers
    also list “N-acetyl Peptide Z-amidate”.
   </Prompt>
   <ExpectedBehavior>
    Answer both parts: what each name means chemically, from authoritative documentation, and how sellers and buyers
    actually use the names, from vendor labels and buyer or specialist discussions, including which variants they tell
    apart and whether they use the short names consistently; a chemistry-only answer states why it skipped the second
    part.
   </ExpectedBehavior>
  </Case>
  <Case id="UnmatchedReplicationNull">
   <Prompt>
    A 16-person study reports a response to right-sided patterned stimulation only in its 8 highly susceptible
    participants; a later blinded, sham-controlled study of 90 people, with a different setup, finds no overall
    effect, and the user asks whether the first result was disproven.
   </Prompt>
   <ExpectedBehavior>
    Reconstruct each study's exact claim: who took part and how susceptible they were, where and how the stimulation
    was given, the control and the outcome; say whether the later study tested the same conditional claim, with its
    full-sample and any subgroup results; report both results, keep the small subgroup result a hypothesis, not
    independent confirmation, and call the effect neither disproven nor established.
   </ExpectedBehavior>
  </Case>
  <Case id="MindfulAuraObservation">
   <Prompt>
    A sense of familiarity can be a seizure aura in some people with epilepsy; a user who sometimes notices that
    sensation asks whether observing it mindfully is risky.
   </Prompt>
   <ExpectedBehavior>
    Keep apart the sensation as a possible symptom of a seizure disorder, the sensation as a cause of seizures, and
    mindful observation as a cause, and support each with its own evidence; mention that it can be a seizure sign only
    as a point about the symptom, not as a risk of the practice; warn against the practice only for a risk shown for
    it, and do not call it risk-free because no risk was found.
   </ExpectedBehavior>
  </Case>
  <Case id="QualifiedLateralityShorthand">
   <Prompt>
    A made-up textbook's diagram says “the right unit is fear-only”, and a later chapter notes that some subjects have
    the two units reversed; a review says the author is unaware of reversed mapping.
   </Prompt>
   <ExpectedBehavior>
    Read the whole text for the author's qualifications before judging the claim; say that the author acknowledges
    reversal, citing both the diagram and the later passage; tell the typical-case shorthand apart from a universal
    claim, criticize only the strongest reading the whole text supports, and test whether the typical-case claim has
    evidence.
   </ExpectedBehavior>
  </Case>
  <Case id="GroupLateralityAverage">
   <Prompt>
    A made-up imaging study finds a mean 2% greater right-side activation during a task, while some participants have
    fully reversed dominance for it; a reviewer calls the right hemisphere the seat of the task in every person.
   </Prompt>
   <ExpectedBehavior>
    Call the finding a group average, which does not show where the function sits in any one person; name the reversed
    participants; say what would show it for an individual, such as a task localizer, stimulation or lesion evidence
    in that person, or an analysis of how many are reversed; do not call the average meaningless.
   </ExpectedBehavior>
  </Case>
